rows.verified: Employers have the same health and safety responsibilities for people working at home as for workers at another workplace.
Employer risk assessments must cover home workers.
Homeworking assessments should consider stress and mental health, computer and laptop use, and the working environment.
A balanced and proportionate approach is appropriate and most homeworking assessments do not require a home visit.
A visit may be appropriate for a disabled worker's special requirements or where tools, chemicals or other significant hazards are involved.
Employers should consider contact arrangements, the type and duration of work, how it can be done safely and any controls required.
Workers cannot be charged for actions needed as a result of the employer's homeworking risk assessment.
If a home is unsuitable and reasonably practicable protections cannot be implemented, an alternative workplace or suitable location should be agreed.
Homeworking controls depend on the job, duration, equipment, home environment, worker needs, communication and emergency arrangements.
Homeworking evidence is worker-, task- and environment-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health or accident probability.
There is no legal maximum working temperature because workplaces and heat-producing processes differ substantially.
Indoor workplaces should normally be at least 16 degrees Celsius, or 13 degrees Celsius where much of the work involves rigorous physical effort.
Employers should provide a reasonable working temperature in workrooms.
Local heating or cooling may be used where a comfortable temperature cannot be maintained throughout a workroom.
Air temperature alone is not a reliable measure of thermal comfort or heat stress.
Thermal comfort assessment should consider air temperature, radiant temperature, air movement, humidity, clothing or PPE and work rate.
Reports of uncomfortable temperatures should prompt the employer to reassess risks, agree actions with workers and act on the findings.
Possible controls include fans, blinds, local heaters, maintained air conditioning, flexible hours, adjusted dress codes and insulation of hot equipment.
Temperature controls depend on indoor or outdoor conditions, work rate, radiant heat, humidity, clothing, worker vulnerability and exposure duration.
Temperature evidence is workplace-, worker- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level heat- or cold-illness probability.
